growth_story.headline: Oman's income per person peaked in 2009 and is now 25.2 percent lower, back near its 1984 level, after oil slumps, a pandemic and caps on oil output.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2010 income per person in Oman grew about 1.3 percent a year and reached its peak in 2009, though the sources read here say little about that long era. Since 2011 it has shrunk by about 1.9 percent a year, starting with falls of 7.8 percent in 2011 and 5.6 percent in 2012, even though the IMF expected strong overall growth in 2011 as public spending and hiring rose. The fall in oil prices from 2014 pushed the budget into deficit, and in 2020 the pandemic and an oil price collapse struck together, so growth averaged -0.9 percent a year over 2016 to 2025, against -0.3 over 2006 to 2015. After a short rebound in 2021 and 2022, income per person fell again from 2023 to 2025 while OPEC+ curbs held back oil output, even as activity outside oil kept growing. By 2025 it was 25.2 percent below the 2009 peak, about where it first was in 1984.

threads.text: In 2011 government spending rose sharply, driven by more public hiring, and the IMF expected strong growth that year. Income per person still fell 7.8 percent in 2011 and 5.6 percent in 2012, the start of the slower era.

threads.title: The oil price fall of 2014
threads.text: When oil prices fell from 2014, the budget and the external accounts moved into deficit, and the IMF warned that large deficits would persist without reform. Income per person fell 3.0 percent in 2014 and 2.9 percent in 2017, with little growth in between.

threads.title: The double shock of 2020
threads.text: In 2020 the pandemic and an oil price collapse hit at once, and the job market adjusted through temporary wage cuts and fewer foreign workers. Income per person fell 1.9 percent that year before rising 3.1 percent in 2021 and 2.7 percent in 2022.

In 2026 conflict in the Middle East hurt logistics and tourism, but access to shipping routes and undamaged energy facilities kept oil, gas and fertilizer exports going, and crude oil output rose. Income per person fell 1.6 percent in 2025, the third fall in a row.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe an economy that was growing: the IMF expected strong growth in 2011, and both the IMF and the World Bank report overall growth in each year from 2023 to 2025. Yet in the data, income per person fell in 2011 and 2012 and again in 2023, 2024 and 2025, by 5.0, 2.8 and 1.6 percent. Output can rise while income per person falls only if the number of people grows faster, but the sources read here do not link the gap to population growth directly.
